questions.q: When an individual consumes alcohol, absorption into the bloodstream occurs primarily across the walls of the stomach and which other organ?
questions.explain: About 20% of alcohol is absorbed through the stomach walls, while the remaining 80% is absorbed through the small intestine.
questions.exam: HOSA Forensic Science: Forensic Toxicology & Pharmacology
questions.subject: Forensic Science

questions.q: The destruction of alcohol (oxidation) in the human body takes place almost entirely in which organ?
questions.explain: Over 90% of ingested ethyl alcohol is oxidized into acetaldehyde and then to acetic acid within the liver.
questions.exam: HOSA Forensic Science: Forensic Toxicology & Pharmacology
questions.subject: Forensic Science

questions.q: What is the primary enzyme responsible for the initial breakdown of ethanol to acetaldehyde in the metabolic pathway: $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} \xrightarrow{\text{Enzyme}} \text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$$ ?
questions.explain: Alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) is the primary enzyme in the liver that oxidizes ethanol into acetaldehyde.
questions.exam: HOSA Forensic Science: Forensic Toxicology & Pharmacology
questions.subject: Forensic Science

questions.q: Although individual variations exist, what is the widely accepted average elimination (burn-off) rate of blood alcohol concentration (BAC) per hour?
questions.explain: The average elimination rate of alcohol is approximately 0.015% w/v (or 0.015 g/dL) per hour.
questions.exam: HOSA Forensic Science: Forensic Toxicology & Pharmacology
questions.subject: Forensic Science

questions.q: In the United States, the legal Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) limit for non-commercial drivers aged 21 and older is universally set at:
questions.explain: Following federal guidelines and standardization across all states, the legal limit for adult non-commercial drivers is 0.08%.
questions.exam: HOSA Forensic Science: Forensic Toxicology & Pharmacology
questions.subject: Forensic Science

questions.q: The scientific foundation of evidential breathalyzers is Henry's Law. At normal body temperature ($34^\circ$C for breath), what is the standard accepted ratio of alcohol in the blood to alcohol in alveolar breath?
questions.explain: Henry's Law states that the concentration of a volatile substance in a liquid is proportional to its concentration in the vapor above it. The standard physiological partition ratio for blood:breath alcohol is 2100 to 1.
questions.exam: HOSA Forensic Science: Forensic Toxicology & Pharmacology
questions.subject: Forensic Science

questions.q: Modern evidential breath testing instruments frequently use which technology to precisely measure alcohol molecules based on how they absorb specific wavelengths of light?
questions.explain: Infrared (IR) spectroscopy measures the absorption of infrared light by the specific chemical bonds in ethanol (C-O and C-H), allowing quantification of alcohol in breath.
questions.exam: HOSA Forensic Science: Forensic Toxicology & Pharmacology
questions.subject: Forensic Science

questions.q: Many portable breathalyzers (PBTs) use fuel cell technology. How does a fuel cell breathalyzer calculate the concentration of alcohol?
options: It oxidizes the alcohol on a platinum electrode, producing a measurable electrical current proportional to the alcohol content.
It changes color from orange to green upon exposure to alcohol, measured by a photometer.
It combusts the breath sample and measures the heat produced.
It records the refraction angle of a laser beam passing through the breath sample.
questions.explain: In a fuel cell, ethanol is oxidized at the anode, releasing electrons. The resulting electrical current is directly proportional to the amount of alcohol in the breath.
questions.exam: HOSA Forensic Science: Forensic Toxicology & Pharmacology
questions.subject: Forensic Science

questions.q: When calculating an individual's theoretical BAC based on the amount of alcohol consumed, which of the following equations is typically used by forensic toxicologists?
questions.explain: The Widmark formula factors in the mass of alcohol consumed, the individual's body weight, and a gender-specific distribution constant to estimate BAC.
questions.exam: HOSA Forensic Science: Forensic Toxicology & Pharmacology
questions.subject: Forensic Science

questions.q: Which factor will most significantly slow the absorption rate of alcohol into the bloodstream?
options: Consuming alcohol with a carbonated mixer.
Having a substantial meal in the stomach prior to drinking.
The ambient temperature of the room.
questions.explain: Food in the stomach slows gastric emptying, thereby delaying the passage of alcohol into the small intestine where maximum absorption occurs.
questions.exam: HOSA Forensic Science: Forensic Toxicology & Pharmacology
questions.subject: Forensic Science

questions.q: Although the liver metabolizes about 90-98% of consumed alcohol, the remaining unmetabolized alcohol is excreted completely unchanged. What are the three primary routes of excretion for this unchanged alcohol?
options: Perspiration, tears, and exhaled carbon dioxide
questions.explain: Between 2% and 10% of alcohol is excreted unchanged in the breath, urine, and sweat (perspiration). This principle allows breath and urine testing to estimate BAC.
questions.exam: HOSA Forensic Science: Forensic Toxicology & Pharmacology
questions.subject: Forensic Science

questions.q: Following absorption, alcohol is distributed uniformly throughout the tissues of the body. Its distribution is directly proportional to the ___ content of the tissues.
questions.explain: Alcohol is highly hydrophilic (water-soluble). It distributes evenly in proportion to the water content of the various body tissues and fluids.
questions.exam: HOSA Forensic Science: Forensic Toxicology & Pharmacology
questions.subject: Forensic Science

questions.q: During a roadside traffic stop, an officer performs a standardized field sobriety test known as HGN. What does HGN stand for?
questions.explain: Horizontal Gaze Nystagmus (HGN) refers to the involuntary jerking of the eyes as they track an object horizontally. Its onset and exaggeration are strongly correlated with intoxication.
questions.exam: HOSA Forensic Science: Forensic Toxicology & Pharmacology
questions.subject: Forensic Science

questions.q: The Walk-and-Turn test and the One-Leg Stand test are standardized field sobriety tasks. Why are these specifically designed as 'divided-attention' tasks?
options: They evaluate muscle strength in both legs independently.
They test the subject's ability to divide physical mass symmetrically.
They require the subject to concentrate on both mental and physical tasks simultaneously, which becomes difficult under the influence of alcohol.
They divide the officer's attention to prevent subjective bias.
questions.explain: Divided attention tasks test the brain's ability to multitask (e.g., balancing while following complex verbal instructions), an ability that is impaired by alcohol.
questions.exam: HOSA Forensic Science: Forensic Toxicology & Pharmacology
questions.subject: Forensic Science

questions.q: For an accurate breathalyzer reading, the instrument must capture 'deep lung' air. What is the anatomical term for the air sacs deep in the lungs where gas exchange occurs?
questions.explain: The alveoli are the terminal air sacs in the lungs where oxygen and carbon dioxide—and volatile substances like alcohol—diffuse into and out of the blood.
